N-1.1-A.skill: compare the number of atoms of one element across samples given as a mass, an amount in moles, and a particle count.

N-1.1-B.skill: identify an unknown element from the number of atoms of another element in a mass of its compound, using the formula to link atoms, moles and molar mass.

N-1.2-A.skill: interpret the molecular-ion peaks of a diatomic element, where each element's isotope abundances must be recovered from a 3-peak pattern, and then compute the average atomic mass.

N-1.2-B.skill: use both the m/z values and the isotope pattern (peak spacing and relative heights) in a mass spectrum to decide how many chlorine or bromine atoms a molecule contains.

N-1.3-A.skill: find a molecular formula from combustion-analysis masses, obtaining oxygen by difference and then scaling the empirical formula using the molar mass.

N-1.3-B.skill: explain why a measured empirical formula deviates from the expected one, using the mass change on forming a nitride versus an oxide and a qualitative observation to rule out a second cause.

N-1.4-A.skill: determine the number of waters of hydration from a heating-to-constant-mass data series, recognizing that only the final constant mass can be used.

N-1.4-B.skill: find the mass percent of one component of a two-component mixture of chlorides from the mass of AgCl precipitated, which requires a two-equation solution rather than assuming one pure component.

N-1.5-A.skill: count unpaired electrons for atoms and ions of d-block elements, including the anomalous half-filled and filled configurations and the rule that 4s electrons are removed first.

N-1.5-B.skill: use successive ionization energies and Coulomb's law to explain how electron-electron shielding within the same shell changes the energy needed to remove an electron.

N-1.6-A.skill: predict how peak positions in a photoelectron spectrum change between isoelectronic species, separating the number of electrons (peak areas) from the nuclear charge (binding energies).

N-1.6-B.skill: identify an element whose photoelectron spectrum reveals an anomalous (non-aufbau) valence configuration, rejecting the element predicted by the usual filling order.

N-1.7-A.skill: identify the number of valence electrons from the position of the largest jump in successive ionization energies and so predict a chloride formula.

N-1.7-B.skill: order the radii of isoelectronic ions by using nuclear charge with a fixed electron count, resisting the trends for neutral atoms.

N-1.8-A.skill: rank the lattice energies of ionic compounds by weighing both ion charges and ion sizes in Coulomb's law, rather than relying on a single factor.

N-1.8-B.skill: combine electron transfer, ionic charges and formula ratios to count ions and transferred electrons in a sample.
